identity.title: Ultrasonic Distance Meter with LCD
identity.tagline: Point it at something, read the distance in centimeters right on a screen.

goal: Build a handheld-style distance meter: an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measures distance to whatever's in front of it, and a 16x2 LCD displays the live reading in centimeters — the first project combining a sensor with a real, human-readable output beyond a single LED.
simpleSummary: Build a handheld gadget that measures and displays distance to whatever's in front of it.
howItWorks: The HC-SR04 measures distance the way sonar does: it emits a short ultrasonic chirp from its TRIG pin, and its ECHO pin goes HIGH for exactly as long as it takes that chirp's echo to bounce back. Since sound travels at a known, roughly constant speed through air, that elapsed time converts directly to a distance. The LCD in this build uses an I2C "backpack" — a small add-on board soldered to the back of the display that lets it be controlled over just two wires (SDA and SCL) instead of the six or more wires a bare LCD normally needs, at the cost of needing one extra library to talk that protocol.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
circuitDiagramCaption: HC-SR04 on D9/D10; LCD on the I2C bus (A4/A5). Both share 5V and GND with the Arduino.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the HC-SR04's VCC to Arduino 5V, GND to GND, TRIG to D9, and ECHO to D10.
wiringSteps.detail: TRIG and ECHO look identical on the module but do opposite jobs — TRIG is an output from the Arduino's perspective, ECHO is an input.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the LCD's I2C backpack: GND to Arduino GND, VCC to 5V, SDA to A4, and SCL to A5.
wiringSteps.detail: A4 and A5 are the Uno's dedicated I2C pins — this is a fixed hardware assignment, not a choice, so double-check you're using exactly these two.

wiringSteps.instruction: Install the LiquidCrystal_I2C library before uploading, and note the I2C address printed on the backpack (commonly 0x27 or 0x3F).
wiringSteps.detail: If the screen shows nothing but garbled or solid blocks, the address in your code not matching your specific backpack's actual address is the most common cause.

code.explanation: readDistanceCm() is the same pulse-timing technique used across every ultrasonic project in this encyclopedia: send a clean trigger pulse, measure how long ECHO stays HIGH, divide by 58 to convert microseconds into centimeters. The main loop simply calls that function repeatedly and reprints the result — lcd.clear() before each update prevents old digits from a longer previous number lingering behind a new, shorter one.

expectedBehavior: The LCD shows a live, continuously updating distance reading in centimeters as you move your hand or an object in front of the sensor.

troubleshooting.issue: LCD shows nothing, or a row of solid blocks.
troubleshooting.fix: Adjust the small contrast potentiometer on the back of the I2C backpack — a completely maladjusted contrast is by far the most common "broken" LCD, and it isn't actually broken.

troubleshooting.issue: LCD backlight is on but no text appears.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the I2C address in your code (0x27 in the example) matches your specific backpack — try 0x3F if 0x27 doesn't work, or run an I2C scanner sketch to find it definitively.

troubleshooting.issue: Distance reading is always -1 or wildly inconsistent.
troubleshooting.fix: Check TRIG and ECHO aren't swapped, and that nothing is within a couple of centimeters of the sensor (its practical minimum range) or beyond about 4 meters (its practical maximum).

extensions: Add a buzzer that beeps faster as an object gets closer, turning this into a simple parking-sensor.
Average several readings together to smooth out noise before displaying.
Log readings over Serial and graph them using the Arduino IDE's Serial Plotter.
Combine this exact sensor code with the Car Counter (2x Ultrasonic) project's dual-sensor logic.
